Name: time_zero_stroke_onset_vs_ball_contact
Title: Stroke onset or ball contact? Whether the time-locked event changes the hit-minus-miss contrast in pre-putt band power
Short Hypothesis: How does the hit-minus-miss contrast in pre-putt band power change when the same putts are time-locked to stroke onset instead of ball contact? Although movement-locked and contact-locked studies are compared as accounts of one preparation period, the hit-minus-miss contrast of band power in the last second differs between epochs time-locked to stroke onset and to ball contact for the same putts, which we conjecture is because the last second before ball contact contains the stroke. What is tested with a pass/fail rule is whether the contrast changes, on putts for which both events are located in a frame-synchronised video; in which bands and regions and in which direction it changes is only estimated, as a map of contrasts under three locks. No simpler route answers it: the two published studies that use different locks also differ in reference, baseline, skill and hole size, and no published table gives contrasts for the same putts under both locks, so the comparison has to be computed on recordings that hold both events.
Related Work: Pre-shot EEG studies of putting compare their outcome effects as findings about one preparation period. Laboratory studies lock the EEG to movement initiation detected at the putter: less frontal-central high-alpha before holed putts (Cooke et al., 2014) [cookeetal2014]; alpha gating before backswing initiation (Gallicchio and Ring, 2018) [gallicchioring2018]; -2 to 0 s before swing onset (Chueh et al., 2025) [chuehetal2025]. Mobile EEG on a green was locked to ball contact by an acoustic trigger because backswing onset could not be detected, and found no alpha difference between holed and missed putts but greater central beta suppression and a frontal theta interaction (Carey et al., 2024) [careyetal2024]. The two kinds of study disagree about the band and also differ in reference, baseline, skill and hole size, so the disagreement cannot be attributed to the lock. [gallicchioring2018] recorded both backswing initiation and impact and analysed one. Stroke timing varies with distance and skill (Dias et al., 2014) [diasetal2014]; (Wu et al., 2020) [wuetal2020], and software event markers have measurable error against a physical reference (Williams et al., 2021) [williamsetal2021]. No retrieved record analyses the same trials under two event definitions (0 hits for four phrasings over 462 records, titles and abstracts only; none of 184 method rows varies the lock). This proposal differs by holding putts, labels, baseline, reference and features fixed and changing only the event. Literature base: 169 screened papers, 10 read in full as plain-text conversions.
Abstract: Studies of pre-shot EEG in golf putting report which frequency band distinguishes successful from unsuccessful putts, and their results are compared as findings about a single preparation period. Yet the studies do not agree on what time zero is. Laboratory work locks the EEG to the start of the stroke, detected by a sensor at the putter; mobile recording on a green locks it to ball contact, because the start of the backswing cannot be detected there. The two kinds of study report different bands, alpha in one case and beta and theta in the other, but they also differ in reference, baseline, skill level and hole size, so nobody can say whether the time-zero definition is responsible. No study has analysed the same putts under both definitions. While that is so, movement-locked and contact-locked findings cannot be reconciled or even compared. We use twelve recordings of four novices putting with a dry-electrode headset, in which a frame-synchronised video lets both stroke onset and ball contact be located for every putt. Holding putts, outcome labels, baseline second, reference and features fixed, we compute the hit-minus-miss contrast of band power in the last second before each event and test whether the two contrasts differ, using a maximum statistic over twelve region-by-band features and a circular-shift null that preserves the serial structure of outcomes. Controls replace true onsets with a constant shift, repeat the analysis with onsets from the head accelerometer, apply the statistic to a window far from the stroke, and plant a known effect. We also test whether stroke duration itself differs by outcome and describe the contrasts under three locks, including the experimenter's key press. The expected contribution is a direct demonstration, on one data set, of whether the choice of time zero alone can change the outcome contrast.
Experiments: E0 [instrument] Trial table, events and rules. Load the 12 PilotDataV2 task recordings with H/M keys (CGX Quick-32r dry headset, 500 Hz, 4 participants, one distance and about 50 putts per recording; /Users/kyc/PythonProject/Golf) with pyxdf; (licence unverified), unpublished laboratory recordings. Ball contact: frame-difference peak in the ball-travel region of the front video within -1 to +4 s of each P key, minus 3 frames, mapped to EEG time by the per-frame LSL stamp. Stroke onset: last moment before ball contact at which motion in the putter region rises above its address-stillness level (median plus 3 robust SD of the preceding 2 s) and stays above it until contact; second detector: the same rule on head-accelerometer jerk. Outcomes: H/M keys paired in order after removing duplicate presses. Decision rules of E2-E7 are committed to git before any outcome analysis; the hash is reported. Compute: estimated 30 min (video decoding).

E1 [descriptive C4] Timing (C4: the intervals between the experimenter's key, stroke onset and ball contact are estimated). Per recording and outcome: P key minus ball contact; stroke onset minus ball contact (video and accelerometer); agreement of the two onset detectors; number of putts without a detectable onset, by outcome. No pass/fail rule. Compute: estimated 5 min.

E2 [tests C1] Contrast under two locks. For every putt cut two time-locked epochs: last second before stroke onset and last second before ball contact; band power by Welch (theta 4-7, alpha 8-12, beta 13-30 Hz; frontal, central, parietal, occipital ROIs; 1-40 Hz zero-phase filter, bad-channel interpolation, average reference) in dB relative to the same baseline second, -5 to -4 s before ball contact. Putts with an onset-to-contact interval above 2 s are dropped and counted, so neither window can reach the baseline; a recording is excluded when the share of putts without a detectable onset differs by more than 10 percentage points between hit and miss. Hit-minus-miss contrast per lock (median within recording, median over recordings within participant, median over participants); T = maximum over the 12 features of the absolute difference between locks. Null: 5,000 circular shifts of the label sequence within recording, applied to both locks together. Decision rule: C1 is refuted if T is at or below the 95th percentile of the null or below 0.5 dB (design choice; the nearest reported outcome difference is 0.484 dB [careyetal2024]). Compute: estimated 15 min.

E3 [control C1] Constant shift. Repeat E2 with pseudo-onsets: ball contact minus the recording's median onset-to-contact interval. If T is as large as in E2, the difference comes from which second is analysed, not from putt-by-putt timing; if it falls inside the null, putt-specific stroke onset matters. Classification rule: pseudo-onset T at least 0.8 of the E2 value means the position of the window explains the difference; below 0.8 means putt-specific timing contributes. This bears on the conjectured reason, not on C1 itself. Compute: estimated 10 min.

E4 [control C1] Onset detector. Repeat E2 and E7 with stroke onset taken from the head accelerometer instead of the video. Rule: if T under accelerometer onsets is inside its null while T under video onsets is not, the result is attributed to the detector and C1 is reported as not supported. Compute: estimated 10 min.

E5 [control C1] Negative control. The statistic of E2 on the second from 2 to 1 s before each event, which precedes the stroke under both locks and cannot reach the baseline second. Expected T inside its null; a T above the null here means outcome-dependent timing error rather than the stroke. Compute: estimated 10 min.

E6 [control C1] Positive control. Plant +1 dB, and separately +0.5 dB, in frontal alpha (fixed in advance) of the onset-locked window of hit putts. Because T takes an absolute value, a planted value returns unchanged only when the unplanted difference of that feature is not negative; its sign and size are reported. The pipeline passes if T exceeds its null and 0.5 dB for the 1 dB plant; the 0.5 dB plant shows whether an effect of the floor's size is detectable. Compute: estimated 10 min.

E7 [tests C2] Stroke duration by outcome (C2: the interval from stroke onset to ball contact separates hit from miss putts). Per recording, AUC of the onset-to-contact interval for hit versus miss putts; hierarchical median of AUC minus 0.5; circular-shift null, two-sided. Decision rule: C2 is refuted if the value is inside the null. Read with E2 and E3: if C2 holds, onset-locked windows of hit and miss putts sit at different distances from contact, and E3's pseudo-onsets show how much of T survives without that. Compute: estimated 5 min.

E8 [descriptive C3] Map under three locks (C3: the contrasts are estimated, not tested - which bands and regions change, in which direction and by how much). Hit-minus-miss contrast of 36 window band power features (three 1-s windows before the event) under the P key, stroke onset and ball contact locks, each with a bootstrap 95% interval over recordings. No pass/fail rule. Compute: estimated 10 min.

E9 [control C1] Movement artifact. Repeat E2 after regressing each band power feature, within recording and lock, on head acceleration (log RMS of the 1-20 Hz accelerometer signal) of the same window. Rule: if T falls inside its null after this adjustment while E2 exceeded it, the difference between locks is attributed to movement in the contact-locked window and reported as such. Compute: estimated 10 min.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Blind restatement unresolved: four participants - data: only 4 participants with keyed recordings exist on this machine.
Blind restatement unresolved: event timing has no physical reference and two detectors may share an error - data: the recordings hold no putter or impact sensor.
Blind restatement unresolved: one unpublished data set and no second data set - data: no second recording with both movement events is on this machine.
Single dataset: no second recording of putting with two movement events is on this machine; the public Carey et al. (2024) set has ball contact only and is not on disk.
Decision rules not externally timestamped: rules are committed to git before any outcome analysis (hash reported); a third party can verify this only if the repository history is shared.

Power: 4 participants (paired d >= 1.24 detectable at 80% power, worse in truth; no literature effect); the tests are permutation statements about these 12 recordings, and a T inside the null says little.

Scope: novices, one dry headset, a taped carpet target; the study shows whether the lock can change the contrast, not why two published studies disagree; the because-clause of C1 is a conjecture; the confirmatory statistic is unsigned, so which band and direction change is only described; (licence unverified) for the laboratory recordings.
Significance not supported by the literature: which event field studies without a putter sensor should report against (third rung of the ladder).
Stroke onset is detected from 30 fps video and head acceleration; novices may start and stop before the stroke; putts with strokes longer than 2 s and recordings with unequal onset loss are dropped.
Regression on head acceleration (E9) can remove neural variance that co-varies with movement.
Literature base: 169 screened papers, 10 read in full as plain-text conversions.
